Subject: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling — follow-up and next steps

Hi Sophie / Tom —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our discovery call + proposed next steps so we have alignment on the performance and autoscaling requirements you raised.

Key customer SLOs you called out:
- Target p95 latency: <= 200 ms for synchronous generation (500 token average).
- Target p99 latency: <= 500 ms (spikes are tolerable short-term, but want <1% breaches).
- Sustained throughput: 800 RPS during business hours; expected burst to 1,500 RPS for up to 20–30 minutes during transaction peaks.
- Concurrent open streaming connections: 400–600 (live transcript streaming for agent UI).
- Streaming response behavior: need token-level partials with <=150 ms first-byte latency for streaming starts.

Autoscaling / capacity expectations you mentioned:
- Burst capacity must be able to absorb 1,500 RPS within ~60–120 seconds from baseline.
- Prefer a warm-pool approach for predictable bursts; cold-starts acceptable for longer tail but should not cause p99 violations.
- Queueing: customer is okay with short queueing (<3s) during extreme bursts but wants backpressure and graceful degradation.

Attachments: I’ve attached the workload profile you shared and our SLO profile sample (redwood_slo_profiles.pdf).

Next steps I propose:
1) Rishi / Connor: can you prepare a one-page feasibility note on warm-pool sizing and expected scale-up time for our recommended model variant (we discussed redwood-llama-13b-quant) — include expected p95/p99 under warm vs cold scenarios.
2) Sophie: please confirm peak windows (dates/times) and whether the burst numbers are for multi-region or single-region (US) traffic.
3) I’ll schedule a quick 30-min follow-up next week to review the feasibility note and proposed quoting for a dedicated burst option.

Thanks —
Marissa

Hi all —

Thanks for the details, Sophie — that helps a lot. Below is a concise feasibility assessment and proposal for how Redwood can meet the SLOs and burst requirements you described.

Short answer: feasible with a mix of pre-warmed capacity + short-term burst reservations + application-level queueing and graceful degradation. Details below.

1) Warm pool sizing and scale-up times
- Recommendation: keep a warm pool sized for ~60% of expected sustained peak (so for 800 RPS sustained, warm pool target ~480 RPS-equivalent capacity). Warm instances are kept hot with KV cache priming and persistent model artifacts so they hit low first-token latency.
- Scale-up: with warm pool + fast provisioning we target scale-to-peak (from warm baseline to 1,500 RPS) in ~45–90s depending on instance types and pre-warm percentage. Without warm pool (cold starts) p99s can spike to multiple seconds.

2) Queueing & backpressure behavior
- Queueing policy: FIFO per-route with SLA-aware drop thresholds. By default we will queue up to 3s of expected processing time; beyond that we surface a 429 with diagnostic payload and optional backoff header for the client.
- Circuit-breakers: yes — we recommend a short window circuit-breaker (15s) plus an adaptive fallback that routes to a smaller model variant when queueing persists. That satisfies your preference for application-level fallback.

3) Streaming specifics
- Streaming first-byte latencies are dominated by tokenizer + model warm state. With warm pool we expect first-byte <= 120–150 ms for the streaming start; cold-token first-byes can be >400 ms.
- Concurrency: 400–600 streaming connections is within the warm pool sizing; we will model memory-backed KV caches for each connection to reduce overhead.

4) Model variants / fallbacks
- Suggest primary = redwood-llama-13b-quant; fallback = redwood-llama-7b-quant or sequence-level response that delivers partials more aggressively. We can embed automatic variant downgrade in the routing policy.

5) Observability & testing before go-live
- We can run a two-week soak with traffic replays from your provided workload profile (fintrax_workload_profile.xlsx). That will let us tune warm pool % and autoscaler thresholds.

6) Pricing / commitment options for burst capacity
- Short-term burst reservation (on-demand reserved credits) for extra warm capacity during known peak windows (e.g., marketing events).
- Dedicated reserved capacity for sustained throughput with agreed SLAs and faster warm pool sizing.

Action items:
- Connor: can you produce a quick sizing table (instances, expected RPS per instance, warm-pool counts) and an estimate of expected p95/p99 under warm vs cold scenarios? Aim to have this by EOD Wed.
- Sophie: confirm whether you want us to run the replay against your production logs (we'll need an S3/transfer link) or a sanitized sample.

Happy to jump on Tue 10:00 PT for the follow-up — Marissa, can you calendar?

— Rishi

Sophie — quick follow-up with the sizing matrix I promised (attached as a table inline here):

- Instance type A (g4-like): ~60 RPS per instance (llama-13b-quant), warm TTFB ~110–150 ms, mem 80GB -> warm pool count for 480 RPS = 8 instances.
- Instance type B (a100-like): ~220 RPS per instance, warm TTFB ~90–120 ms -> warm pool count for 480 RPS = 3 instances.
- Cold-start penalty: expect +300–1200 ms added to p99 depending on image pull & model cold-load.

Practical plan:
1) Start with a mixed warm pool (2 x A + 1 x B) that gives ~340 RPS warm baseline, then use short-term burst credits to spin additional B instances for peak windows. This gives a trade-off between cost and speed.
2) Autoscaler policy: aggressive ramp-up thresholds (scale-up at 65% CPU/KV saturation) with short cool-downs; queueing allowed up to 3s then downgrade.
3) Testing: we recommend two test runs — one with warm pool pre-primed and one simulating cold starts so we can measure p99 sensitivity.

I attached the spreadsheet with the full numbers (fintrax_workload_profile.xlsx). Let me know if you want the raw numbers as a CSV.
